catalog_quote: Stress is usually, but not always, on the first syllable of a word. We have evidence of this both in my own recordings of speakers today, in Wurm's data, and also in Roth's data. Roth meticulously marks syllable boundaries of every word by hyphens, and underlines the stressed syllable. Holmer (1983:457) notes that stress is not contrastive, adding that 'the usual tendency toward stressing of the second initial syllable in long words or sequences prevails: nganádhuru (bagu) '(to) all of us', nganádhurunga 'us all', bundálbaringi 'brought' (my orthography). Roth cites a few polysyllabic words with non-initial stress (e.g. noo-râng-ûn nurángan 'star' from Rosewood 1898:73). He also, intriguingly, gives the forms for clearly cognate words from different Dharumbal areas which seem to differ in their stress placement: 'sun' Torilla kâ-rĕ gári / Rosewood kâ-rā gará (Roth 1898:73; my phonemicis…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Dharumbal (dhar1248) is not in the catalog. Both search title-hits are Glottolog mis-attributions (a Central Mexican Spanish focus-intonation chapter and an English L1/L2 nuclear-accent study); neither concerns Dharumbal and both were judged from their Crossref abstracts. The real stress evidence was obtained instead: Terrill 2002 (Pacific Linguistics 525), open at the ANU repository (CC BY-SA) and archive.org, states in §3.6 (p. 24) that stress is usually but not always initial, that Holmer found it non-contrastive with second-syllable stress in long words, and that phonemicity is unresolved; Holmer 1983 (PL D-54, p. 457, also open at ANU) was downloaded and confirms the quoted first-hand statement. our earlier reading classification 'the named source could not be reached' for Terrill 2002 is now obsolete (handle 1885/146146).org APIs.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress typically falls on the first syllable; Terrill treats it as non-contrastive in practice but leaves phonemicity open. Holmer (1983:457, one Keppel Island speaker) says stress is not distinctive and that longer words tend to carry stress on the second syllable (ŋanáDuru, bundálbariŋi), which Terrill reports as a divergent observation rather than the general rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Roth (1898) records a few polysyllables with non-initial stress (nurángan 'star') and cognate forms differing in stress between Torilla (gári) and Rosewood (gará) 'sun'; Holmer reports second-syllable prominence in words of three or more syllables (his §17.2 links it to lengthening of the second vowel). Terrill: 'not clear.. whether or not stress was phonemic'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms from old wordlists, Wurm's 1955 elicitation tape, and Terrill's own recordings of present-day speakers); Holmer's remark covers 'long words or sequences'. The language is dormant/near-extinct; the description rests on thin and heterogeneous data from several dialect areas (Kuinmabara/Torilla, Karunbara/Rosewood, Rakiwara/Yeppoon, Tarumbal/Rockhampton, Wapabara/Keppel Islands).
new_statements.identity_note: Terrill 2002 covers Dharumbal as a whole (glottocode dhar1248, ISO xgm), pooling data from the Roth 1897 dialect wordlists (Kuinmabara, Karunbara, Rakiwara, Tarumbal, Wapabara), Wurm's 1955 tape and modern rememberers; Holmer 1983's 'Darumbal' chapter describes the Keppel Island (Wapabara/Ganumi) variety of a single speaker, Mrs Kanomie Richards, which Terrill treats as one of the Dharumbal dialects. No separate glottocodes exist for these dialects in Glottolog.

new_statements.reading: Default word-initial stress (first syllable), with attested exceptions: Holmer's Keppel Island informant stressed the second syllable of long (4-5 syllable) words (ŋanáDuru, bundálbariŋi), Roth's 1898 wordlists show a few non-initial stresses (nurángan 'star') and dialect-dependent placement (ká-rë vs ka-rá 'sun'), and Terrill leaves contrastiveness open. For a catalog's classification this is 'initial (fixed, non-contrastive) with reported variation'; the language is currently not in the catalog, so this would be a new entry, not a supersession. Holmer 1983:457 is the first-hand source behind the second-syllable remark and was read directly.

sources.quote: 17.4 Although stress is not distinctive in Darumbal, the usual tendency toward stressing of the second initial syllable in long words or sequences prevails: ŋanáDuru (bagu) (to) all of us, ŋanáDuruŋa us all, bundálbariŋi brought.
sources.locator: Part III, Phonology §17.4, p. 457 (PDF p. 465); see also §17.2 p. 457
sources.note: §17.4: 'Although stress is not distinctive in Darumbal, the usual tendency toward stressing of the second initial syllable in long words or sequences prevails: ŋanáDuru (bagu) (to) all of us, ŋanáDuruŋa us all, bundálbariŋi brought.' §17.2 adds that in ŋanaDuru the second a is lengthened 'concomitant with a slight stress on the second initial syllable'. Based on one speaker (Mrs Kanomie Richards, North Keppel Island). Part II §9.6 gives the same author's blanket claim that stress is not distinctive in all Australian languages he studied.

Bibliographic only: lists Terrill 2002 as the description; 25 alternative names; no dialect children. The other three refs in our exported Glottolog list (Cooper 2019 Barnsley dialect; Dyer & Beckford-Wassink 2001; Casad & Palmer 2003) are false matches on an alternative name and are not about Dharumbal.
